
# Notation
***

This appendix collects every symbol this book uses, so you have one place to look when a formula in a later chapter reuses a letter from an earlier one.
It describes this book's choices, since there is no universal standard.
Statistics notation varies by field, by textbook, and sometimes by chapter within one textbook.
Expect other sources to write the sample mean as $\bar{x}$ where this book writes $\hat{m}$, and to use $P(\cdot)$ where this book uses $\text{Prob}(\cdot)$.
Throughout, a hat marks a quantity computed from data, and a bare letter marks the theoretical quantity it corresponds to.
Once you have that, most formulas can be read before you know the details, because the decoration tells you whether you are looking at something you can compute or something you can only estimate.
The tables below are grouped by topic in roughly the order the book introduces them.

## Hats and No Hats

The book distinguishes the **sample** (the data you observed) from the **population** (the theoretical quantity you want to know) using hats.

For example, $M$ estimates the population mean $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]$ and varies across samples, while $\hat{m}$ is the one number from your sample data.
We use lowercase letters under the hat for sample quantities, including the mean $\hat{m}$, variance $\hat{v}$, standard deviation $\hat{s}$, proportion $\hat{p}(x)$, covariance $\hat{c}_{XY}$, and correlation $\hat{r}_{XY}$.
The mean, variance, and standard-deviation estimators are $M$, $V$, and $S$ before the sample is observed.
Observed values of the random variables $X_{i}$ and $Y_{i}$ are written $\hat{x}_{i}$ and $\hat{y}_{i}$.
Without a subscript, $\hat{x}=(\hat{x}_{1}, \ldots, \hat{x}_{n})$ and $\hat{y}$ denote the whole vector of observed values, as in "the variance of $\hat{x}$".
The superscript $\mathrm{pred}$ marks a model's prediction: $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)$ is its prediction at a design point $x$.
The superscript $\mathrm{fit}$ marks a fitted value: $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}=\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(\hat{x}_{i})$ is the model's prediction for the observed outcome $\hat{y}_{i}$.
Uppercase variable labels in subscripts identify which variables a statistic describes: $\hat{c}_{XY}$ is the sample covariance of $\hat{x}$ and $\hat{y}$.
Conventional names retain their capitals: $\hat{F}$ denotes an empirical CDF or an F-statistic, $\hat{U}$ is the Mann--Whitney statistic, and $\hat{R}^2$ is the coefficient of determination.
Abbreviations such as $\hat{\text{SE}}$, $\hat{\text{IQR}}$, and $\hat{\text{RSS}}$ also retain their capitals.

In R code, observed sample values use `x_hat` and `y_hat` (or `xy_hat` for a pair), and simulated draws use `x_sim` (or `xy_sim`).
Their mean, variance, standard deviation, and median use `m_hat`, `v_hat`, `s_hat`, and `med_hat`.
For example, `x_hat[i]` corresponds to $\hat{x}_{i}$ and `med_hat` to $\tilde{m}$.
Fitted values use `y_fit`, predictions at design points use `y_pred`, and residuals use `e_hat`, so `e_hat <- y_hat - y_fit` matches the residual identity.
Empirical CDFs use `F_hat` in code, while kernel density estimates and stored histograms use `f_hat`, matching $\hat{F}(x)$ and $\hat{f}(x)$.
See [Code Conventions](04_B_CodeStyle.qmd#assignment-and-naming) for naming groups, bootstrap replicates, and matrices.

The table below pairs sample quantities with their population or theoretical counterparts.

| Concept | Sample (data) | Population (theory) |
|---|---|---|
| Observation | $\hat{x}_{i}$, $\hat{y}_{i}$ | $X_{i}$, $Y_{i}$ |
| Cumulative Distribution Function | $\hat{F}(x)$, ECDF | $F(x)=\text{Prob}(X_{i} \leq x)$ |
| Probability Density Function (continuous) | $\hat{f}(x)$, histogram or kernel density | $f(x)$ |
| Proportion | $\hat{p}(x)$ | $p(x)=\text{Prob}(X_{i} = x)$ |
| Mean | $\hat{m}$ | $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]$ |
| Variance, Std deviation | $\hat{v}$, $\hat{s}$ | $\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]$, $\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}$ |
| Adjusted variance, Std deviation | $\hat{v}_{\text{adj}}$, $\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}$ | $\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]$, $\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}$ |
| Quantile at probability $p$ | $\hat{q}(p)=\hat{F}^{-1}(p)$ | $F^{-1}(p)$ |
| Median | $\tilde{m}=\hat{F}^{-1}(0.5)$ | $F^{-1}(0.5)$ |
| Interquartile range | $\hat{\text{IQR}}=\hat{F}^{-1}(0.75)-\hat{F}^{-1}(0.25)$ | $F^{-1}(0.75)-F^{-1}(0.25)$ |
| Joint probability | $\hat{p}(x, y)$ | $p(x, y) = \text{Prob}(X_{i} = x ~\text{and}~ Y_{i} = y)$ |
| Conditional probability | $\hat{p}(y \mid x)$ | $p(y \mid x) = \text{Prob}(Y_{i} = y \mid X_{i} = x)$ |
| Conditional mean function | $\hat{m}_{Y}(x,h)$, mean of $\hat{y}_{i}$ for $\hat{x}_{i}$ within window $[x-h, x+h]$; $\hat{m}_{Y}(x)$ when $x$ is a category (exact match, no bandwidth) | $m_{Y}(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i} \mid X_{i}=x]$ |
| Conditional quantile | $\hat{F}_{Y}^{-1}(p \mid x)$, $p$ quantile of $\hat{y}_{i}$ for $\hat{x}_{i}=x$ | $F_{Y}^{-1}(p \mid x)$ |
| Covariance | $\hat{c}_{XY}$ | $\mathbb{C}[X_{i}, Y_{i}]$ |
| Correlation | $\hat{r}_{XY}$ | $\mathbb{C}[X_{i},Y_{i}]/\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]\mathbb{V}[Y_{i}]}$ |
| Regression coefficient | $\hat{b}_{k}$ | $\beta_{k}$ |
| Residual / error | $\hat{e}_{i}$ | $\epsilon_{i}$ |

Note that $\mathbb{E}$, $\mathbb{V}$, and $\mathbb{C}$ are functions computed only on random variables.
We write population means, variances, and standard deviations as $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]$, $\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]$, and $\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]}$ throughout the book.
The argument identifies the random variable: $\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]$ describes individual observations, while $\mathbb{V}[M]$ describes the sample mean across samples.
Distribution parameters keep their own names, such as $\theta$ for a Bernoulli distribution and $\lambda$ for a Poisson distribution (with $\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=\mathbb{V}[X_{i}]=\lambda$).
Similarly, we reserve $\mu$ and $\sigma$ for the [Normal](01_04_RandomVariables.qmd#normal-gaussian) distribution.

## Indices and Sub/Superscripts

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $_{i}$ | Observation in sample or population ( $i = 1, \ldots, n, n + 1, \ldots N$) | $\hat{x}_{i}$ is value of the $i$th observation |
| $_{j}$ | Secondary observation index (pairwise sums only) | $\sum_{j \neq i} \hat{x}_{j}$ |
| $_{k}$ | Variable index in $K$ variables ($k=1,\ldots,K$) | $\hat{b}_{k}$, $\hat{x}_{ik}$ |
| $_{g}$ |  Group index in $G$ groups ($g=1,\ldots,G$) | $\hat{m}_{Y}(g)$ |
| $^*$ | Optimal or equilibrium value | $P^*$, equilibrium price |
| $^{(b)}$ | Bootstrap replicate | $\hat{x}_{i}^{(b)}$, $\hat{m}^{(b)}$ |
| $^{\mathrm{fit}}$ | Fitted value, the prediction at a sample point | $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ |
| $^{\mathrm{pred}}$ | Prediction at a design point | $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)$ |
| $^{(-i)}$ | Leave-one-out replicate, omitting observation $i$ | $\hat{m}^{(-i)}$, $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{j})$ |
| $^{\text{boot}~,~ \text{jack}}$ | Bootstrap, Jackknife variant | $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{boot}}$, $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{jack}}$ |
| $_{\text{adj}}$ | Adjusted for degrees of freedom | $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}$, $\hat{s}_{\text{adj}}$ |
| $_{0}$ | Null hypothesis | $\hat{F}_{0}$ |

In $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}(-i)}(\hat{x}_{j})$, the argument $\hat{x}_{j}$ identifies the observation being predicted, and the superscript $(-i)$ identifies the observation omitted from the fit.

The letter $g$ has two uses, distinguished by how it is written.
As an index, $g$ labels groups, as in $\hat{y}_{ig}$ and $\hat{m}_{Y}(g)$.
Written with its own argument, $g(x)$ is any function, as in $\mathbb{E}[g(X_{i})]$ from [LOTUS](01_06_EstimationTheory.qmd#law-of-the-unconscious-statistician-lotus).
With a hat, $\hat{g}$ is a function of the observed data, so it can be any statistic, such as $\hat{m}$ or $\tilde{m}$.
Then $\hat{g}_{1}$ and $\hat{g}_{2}$ are that statistic computed in group 1 and group 2.

## Regression 

Fitted simple regression:

$$\hat{y}_{i} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1} \hat{x}_{i} + \hat{e}_{i}$$

Fitted local linear regression at $x$:

$$\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x) = \hat{b}_{0}(x,h) + \hat{b}_{1}(x,h)x$$

Here $\hat{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}(x)$ is the prediction at $x$, and the local coefficients depend on $x$ and the bandwidth $h$.

Fitted multiple regression:

$$\hat{y}_{i} = \sum_{k=0}^{K} \hat{b}_{k} \hat{x}_{ik} + \hat{e}_{i}$$

Here $\hat{x}_{i0}=1$ supplies the intercept, $\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\hat{b}_{k}\hat{x}_{ik}$ is the fitted value, and $\hat{e}_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}^{\mathrm{fit}}$ is the fitted sample residual.
In least-squares minimization, lowercase $b_{k}$ denotes a trial coefficient, and $\hat{e}_{i}=\hat{y}_{i}-\sum_{k=0}^{K}b_{k}\hat{x}_{ik}$ depends on those trial values until the fit is chosen.
The coefficient estimator $B_{k}$ varies across samples, while $\hat{b}_{k}$ is its value in the observed sample and $\beta_{k}$ is the population coefficient it estimates.
The population error $\epsilon_{i}$ is an unobserved random disturbance, whereas the sample residual $\hat{e}_{i}$ is computed from the fitted model.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $b_{0}$, $b_{k}$ | Trial intercept and coefficients in minimization |
| $B_{k}$ | Coefficient estimator before seeing data |
| $\hat{b}_{k}$, $\hat{b}_{k}(x, h)$ | Fitted intercept, coefficient |
| $\beta_{k}$, $\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x})$  | Population coefficient, marginal effect at $\mathbf{x}$ |
| $h$ or $h_{k}$ | Bandwidth (half-width of a window around $x$) |
| $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$ | Indicator function |
| $k(\hat{x}_{i}, x, h)$ | Kernel weight function |
| $W(x)$, $w(x)$ | Unnormalized weight, normalized weight ($\sum_{x} w(x) = 1$) |
| $W_{i}$, $w_{i}$ | Unnormalized weight, normalized weight of observation $i$ ($\sum_{i} w_{i} = 1$) |
| $\epsilon_{i}$ | Population error term |
| $\hat{e}_{i}$ | Sample residual |
| $\hat{\text{MSE}}$ | Mean squared error, the average of $\hat{e}_{i}^2$ |
| $\hat{s}^2_{\text{adj}}$ | Adjusted mean squared error, the sum of $\hat{e}_{i}^2$ divided by $n-K-1$ |
| $\hat{R}^2$ | Coefficient of determination |
| $\hat{R}^2_{\text{adj}}$ | Adjusted R-squared |

Bold $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ collects the fitted coefficients, and bold $\hat{\mathbf{e}}$ collects the sample residuals.
In contingency tables, $\hat{e}_{kj}$ instead denotes an expected cell count; the context and indices distinguish it from a regression residual.

The letter $h$ is a *half-width* everywhere it appears, measured from a point $x$ out to the edge of the window.
So a histogram bin is $2h$ wide, a kernel gives zero weight once $|\hat{x}_{i}-x| > h$, and a local regression at $x$ fits on the observations within $h$ of it.
These are all the same idea, which is how much data around a point gets used.
LOESS is the one exception: its `span` fixes the *share* of observations in each window instead of the width, so the window widens where data are sparse rather than staying at a fixed $h$.

The letter $k$ does double duty here, distinguished by whether it takes arguments.
A bare subscript $k$ is the variable index, so $h_{k}$ is the bandwidth for variable $\hat{x}_{k}$ and $\hat{b}_{k}(\mathbf{x})$ is the marginal effect of that variable at the point $\mathbf{x}$.
Written with arguments, $k(\cdot)$ is the kernel weight function.
Capital $K$ is the number of explanatory variables, and bold $\mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x})$ is the matrix of kernel weights.

## Hypothesis Testing and Sampling

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\hat{g}$, $\hat{g}_{1}$, $\hat{g}_{2}$ | Any sample statistic, such as $\hat{m}$ or $\tilde{m}$; that statistic in group 1 or group 2 |
| $\hat{m}$, $\hat{d}$, $\hat{b}_{k}$ | Estimate of the population mean (realized, after seeing data), difference in a statistic between two groups ($\hat{g}_{1}-\hat{g}_{2}$), or regression coefficient |
| $\text{SE}(M)$, $\text{SE}(D)$, $\text{SE}(B_{k})$ | Theoretical standard error of the estimators |
| $\hat{\text{SE}}(M)$, $\hat{\text{SE}}(D)$, $\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{k})$ | Estimated standard error of the estimator |
| $\hat{m}^{(b)}$, $\hat{m}^{(-i)}$ | Bootstrap replicate, Jackknife (Leave-one-out)  mean |
| $\hat{m}^{\text{boot}}$, $\hat{m}^{\text{jack}}$ | Mean of the bootstrap or jackknife distribution |
| $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{boot}}$,  $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{jack}}$ | Bootstrap, Jackknife method of standard error estimate |
| $\hat{t}$, $\hat{z}$, $\hat{F}$  | t-statistic, z-statistic, F-statistic |
| $H_{0}$, $H_{A}$ | Null, Alternative hypothesis |
| $m_{0}$ | Hypothesized population mean in $H_{0}:\mathbb{E}[X_{i}]=m_{0}$ |
| $q(\alpha/2)$ | Critical quantile |

For a regression coefficient estimator, $\text{SE}(B_{k})=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[B_{k}]}$, and $\hat{\text{SE}}(B_{k})$ is its estimate computed from data.
The method can be specified as $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{boot}}(B_{k})$ or $\hat{\text{SE}}^{\text{jack}}(B_{k})$.
